title: The dandy’s warning
where: *Intimate Journals*: *Rockets*, XIII and XXVI; *My Heart Laid Bare*, LXXII and LXXIX
about: Baudelaire writes these notes to himself on loose sheets in about his last ten years. He has a stroke in 1866 and dies in 1867; the notes are printed after his death, in the order his publisher pasted them. The first passage is from the last entry of *Rockets*, which says the world is ending and foretells an age that honors only money. The other two are from late entries of *My Heart Laid Bare* that begin with the word *Hygiene*; beside the third stands a maxim from *Rockets*, XIII.

view.says: Auden reads the journals through Baudelaire’s dandy, whose one ambition is to become conscious that he is uniquely himself and like no one else. A thought contrary to the dandy, he says, runs through them from the start: to love is to give oneself where a neighbor needs it. It seems to surface only now and then before the crisis of January 23, 1862. After it he finds the heart truly changed.
view.quote: a man fighting against time to eradicate a lifetime’s habits of thought and feeling, and set himself in order and acquire a history
view.source: Introduction to Charles Baudelaire, *Intimate Journals*, translated by Christopher Isherwood (Hollywood: Marcel Rodd, 1947), pp. 18–20 and 25–27; the closing pages are also in *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 314–15

One word was changed: until became before

lenses.label: Likeness
lenses.name: simile
lenses.plain: a comparison that says one thing is like another; here the word is *as*
lenses.caption: The writer likens himself to someone, I am as a tired man, and keeps the man. The next sentence is about that man: he speaks, the me in the quotation is his, and no I comes back before the paragraph ends. The French does the same: un homme, cet homme, il. So the pride of the last lines is told of a third person, and by comparison: he is proud of being less base than the people who pass. Auden lists this pride among the dandy’s traits. The dandy’s mistake, he says, is to think one becomes an individual in spirit by becoming unlike other people.
lenses.why: The simile turns I into a man and keeps him, so his pride is told of a third person, by comparison with the passers-by; Auden calls it the dandy’s mistake to seek individuality in being unlike others.

grounds.claim: the chain from I to as a tired man, that man, he and me; the same chain in the French of the pair (un homme, cet homme, il); the phrase of pride, words 107 to 115, qualifies he and is a comparative, less base than
a simile is a comparison of two things in which both are mentioned and the comparison is stated outright
grounds.source: Online Etymology Dictionary, simile

lenses.label: Delay
lenses.caption: The last sentence opens with a time, The evening, and forty-nine words pass before its main clause, the part that could stand alone. After the clause of time come six phrases, each headed by a word that describes the man: cradled, forgetful, content, resigned, intoxicated, proud. A handbook of composition calls this suspense: describing words set before their subject keep the sentence incomplete and throw the emphasis on its end. Six states come first, the main verb is he said, and the end is his question. In the other journal Baudelaire writes A dandy does nothing. Auden calls the dandy no man of action.
lenses.why: Six describing phrases set before their subject hold the sentence open for forty-nine words and throw the emphasis on its end, his question; Baudelaire writes that a dandy does nothing, and Auden’s dandy is no man of action.

grounds.claim: where the main clause stands; the six phrases before it; forty-nine words from The evening to passed, the two pairs of words joined by dashes counted as two each
the French of the pair has the same six phrases in the same order: bercé, oublieux, content, résigné, enivré, fier

a participle or adjective that qualifies the subject, set before the subject, gains suspense, and an excessive use of it is French (Abbott, rule 33); in suspense the reader feels the sentence incomplete until the full stop, and one way to it is to place participles before the words they qualify (rule 30); suspense throws increased emphasis on the words waited for, that is, on the end of the sentence (the remark that closes rule 30 a); the end of a sentence is an emphatic position, mostly more so than the beginning (rules 15 and 16); the emphatic words of a sentence belong at the end, and a periodic sentence gives prominence to its main statement (Strunk, rule 18)
grounds.source: Edwin A. Abbott, How to Write Clearly: Rules and Exercises on English Composition (Boston: Roberts Brothers, 1883), rules 15, 16, 30, 30 a and 33, read in Project Gutenberg no. 22600; William Strunk, Jr., The Elements of Style (New York: Harcourt, Brace, 1920; its title page gives copyright 1918 and 1919 to the author and 1920 to the publisher), rule 18, read in Project Gutenberg no. 37134

grounds.claim: the main clause of a sentence is the clause that its phrases and dependent clauses come before or after; a clause that does not depend on another is grammatically complete and can be written as a sentence by itself
grounds.source: William Strunk, Jr., The Elements of Style (1920), rules 3 and 5, read by the finisher on 2026-10-03 in Project Gutenberg no. 37134 (lines 333–335 and 421–433 of the e-text): rule 3 sets the main clause against the phrases and dependent clauses before or after it, and rule 5 calls independent clauses grammatically complete and allows them to be written as separate sentences. Opened for the plain words the critic added to the first sentence of the caption (critic.md, change 3)

lenses.caption: Sangfroid is French for cool blood: in Littré’s dictionary, calm of soul, presence of mind. Intoxicated translates the French enivré, made drunk, and Littré adds a figurative sense: a moral drunkenness, as on praise. The phrase makes one man drunk on his own calm. It joins two terms that seem to contradict each other: the figure is called an oxymoron. Dandyism is built on an English word that French borrowed about 1830; Littré’s dandy is a man who carries the fashions to the point of ridicule. Auden says Baudelaire’s dandy looks to the bourgeois like a man of every excess and to himself like an exacting ascetic.
lenses.why: Intoxicated with his sangfroid joins drunkenness to cool blood, two terms that seem to contradict, in one man; Auden says Baudelaire’s dandy is a figure of every excess to the bourgeois and an exacting ascetic to himself.

lenses.label: French

ties.say: The French is *he says to himself*: the tense is present, and the verb turns back on the speaker. Shipley’s *he said* is past and leaves out *to himself*.
The French is *those who pass*, in the present. The past tense is Shipley’s.

The French is *has stolen*, a compound past that looks back from the present of *he says*. Shipley’s *stole* puts the theft in a finished past. *Destinée* is the word he translates as *destiny* in the third passage.
*Sang-froid* goes over unchanged: English has had the phrase since 1712. *Dandysme* is the English word *dandy* with a French ending.
The aside is Baudelaire’s own and Shipley keeps it. This copy of the French has lost the first of its two dashes; the Paris edition of 1908 prints both.

lenses.caption: Shipley keeps Baudelaire’s order phrase for phrase and moves the last sentence into the past. Baudelaire writes a volé, has stolen, passent, pass, and il se dit, he says to himself: the time is the present. Shipley writes stole, passed and he said, and leaves out to himself. So in the French he asks himself, now, why it should matter to him where these consciences go. The paragraph opens by disclaiming the charity of a doctor, and Littré’s first sense of charité is love of one’s neighbor. The thought contrary to the dandy, Auden says, is that to love is to give oneself where a neighbor needs it.
lenses.why: In the French the man asks himself, now, what it matters where these consciences go; the writer has disclaimed charity, love of one’s neighbor; the thought contrary to the dandy, Auden says, is that to love is to give oneself.

grounds.claim: the same order of phrases in both; a volé, passent and il se dit against stole, passed and he said

lenses.label: Time
lenses.caption: The first sentence says always. The second paragraph says Now, and always again, and then the time narrows to to-day and a date. No other entry in Shipley’s translation of the two journals gives the day on which it was written. The verbs change at the date. Before it stands something he has done: he has cultivated his hysteria. After it the verb is felt, twice, and what he feels passes over me. Baudelaire’s first verb there is subi, underwent. Auden calls this day the crisis. In another essay he writes that Baudelaire’s pose led to disaster, to his hearing this wind, as Baudelaire himself saw too late.
lenses.why: The time narrows from always to now to one dated day, and at the date the verbs pass from what he has done to what he undergoes; Auden calls the day the crisis.

lenses.label: Wing
lenses.name: metaphor
lenses.plain: one thing spoken of as another
lenses.caption: The entry does not say what happened. This metaphor gives imbecility a wing. Imbecility itself stays two steps off: what he feels is a gust, the gust is from the wing, and the wing is imbecility’s. So what reaches him is moving air, and he calls it a warning. His sonnet “Le Gouffre,” The Gulf, has the wind and no wing: the wind of Fear, felt mainte fois, many a time. Auden quotes the entry as the crisis, and the last lines of his introduction have a bird: as Baudelaire spoke, it came down and struck.
lenses.why: The metaphor keeps imbecility two steps off: he feels only a gust from its wing and calls it a warning; Auden quotes the entry as the crisis, and his last lines have a bird that strikes.

lenses.caption: Cultivated is a farmer’s verb: Littré’s first sense of cultiver is to work the land so that it bears, and a later one is to form and develop. Its object here is a disease: in Littré, a nervous illness that comes in fits. So the entry presents the hysteria as his own work, done with joy and terror; then, with Now, come vertigo and the wing of imbecility. Auden takes up the phrase in two essays. A religion that trusts the mood of the moment leads first to this cultivation, he writes, and at last to despair; Baudelaire’s error, he says, was to make the aesthetic his religion.
lenses.why: The verb makes the hysteria his own work; Auden says a religion that trusts the mood of the moment leads first to this cultivation and at last to despair, and that Baudelaire made the aesthetic his religion.

grounds.claim: cultiver: first to work the land so that it produces; figuratively to cultivate an art, a science, the virtues; then to form, to develop, with examples of cultivating hatred and fury
grounds.source: Littré, cultiver, senses 1, 2 and 3

grounds.claim: hystérie: a term of medicine, a nervous disease that shows itself in fits, marked by convulsions, the sensation of a ball rising from the womb to the throat, and suffocation
grounds.source: Littré, hystérie

lenses.label: Maxim

ties.say: The maxim meets any creditor, at each letter. The budget has three names, a sum against each, and a total by the month.
The maxim orders writing and counts it in lines: fifty, on an abstract subject. The budget orders work and counts it by the clock, from six till noon.
The maxim promises: *you are saved*. Baudelaire’s French has the future, *you will be saved*. The budget promises nothing: *we shall see*.

lenses.caption: Auden sets these two notes side by side: the writer of the maxim now writes the budget. The maxim is one sentence, said to anyone, you, for each letter. It speaks of no payment: the letter is met with fifty lines written on a subject the French calls extra-terrestre, outside the earth, and you are saved. The budget begins with two other people, Jeanne Duval (Jean) and his mother, and their monthly sums; then come hours of work. Its first paragraph ends We shall see the result. Auden says these last pages show him racing time to undo the habits of a lifetime and put his life in order.
lenses.why: Auden sets the two notes together as one man’s, before and after: the maxim answers a creditor’s letter with lines on nothing earthly and says you are saved; the budget counts money for two other people and hours of work.

grounds.claim: the writer of the maxim about the creditor now writes the budget; the last pages show him racing time to undo the habits of a lifetime and put his life in order. Of this leaf Auden quotes the line of names and sums, and then resolutions from other leaves (to work at once, a prayer, his earnings divided in four, sobriety); his maxim, in Isherwood’s words, keeps the unearthly subject and the future tense of the French
grounds.source: W. H. Auden, Introduction to Charles Baudelaire, Intimate Journals, translated by Christopher Isherwood (Hollywood: Marcel Rodd, 1947), pp. 25–26; the same passage in Prose, vol. II, p. 314, read by the examiner from the head of that page to its foot in the archive.org search snippets on 2026-10-03

lenses.label: Verbs
lenses.caption: The account has no verb: three names, three sums, a total. The two resolutions begin To work. The infinitive names an act and fixes no person, so no one is yet said to do the work. The first verb with a person is plural and future: We shall see. The first I only supposes: I suppose. Then the plain present: There is still time. In French the entry before this one begins, after its heading, Trop tard peut-être, too late perhaps, words Shipley’s text lacks. Auden’s introduction ends on the same question. By nature’s reckoning, he writes, Baudelaire was too late; by the spirit’s, one may believe, he came in time.
lenses.why: The note moves from verbless sums and infinitives with no person to We shall see, I suppose and There is still time; Auden ends on it: too late by nature’s reckoning; by the spirit’s, one may believe, in time.

lenses.caption: Three words come back from the first passage. There the man stole a few hours of pleasure from fate. Here he supposes he bases his destiny on a few hours of toil. Fate and destiny are one French word, destinée, and heures, hours, is in both sentences, so work stands where pleasure stood. Five entries earlier he names pleasure and work as the two ways to forget time and writes Let us choose. Pleasure then returns twice: in a question that breaks off, and as the pleasure of a project carried out, which he has not yet known. Auden says the heart has really changed between the dandy and what these last pages resolve.
lenses.why: Fate, hours and pleasure return from the first passage with work where pleasure stood, and five entries earlier he names the two and writes Let us choose; Auden says the heart has really changed since the dandy.

auden.says: Auden says that Baudelaire met his own nature and his century with two opposed figures of his own making, and held to them until shortly before his mind gave way: the dandy, the individual as hero, and the mass, which he thought boorish and found in Woman, in the man of business and in what he called the Belgian spirit. Auden then lists the dandy’s traits from the journals: he lives and sleeps before a looking glass, does nothing useful, is solitary and unhappy, and is proud of being less base than the people passing. That last trait is taken from the second sentence of the first passage.
auden.source: Introduction to Charles Baudelaire, *Intimate Journals* (1947), pp. 18–19
auden.checked: research notes, remake/research/C_auden_on_works.md, appendix H5; and the search snippets of the 1947 edition at archive.org, read again on 2026-10-03: the running head of page 19 falls inside the sentence about the opposites, the list follows it, and the head of page 20 comes after the list. Read again by the examiner the same day: the sentence on the pair of opposites and both lists, item by item; and once more before closing, backward from the opposites to the start of that sentence (Baudelaire, faced with his own nature and the society of his century, devised the pair and kept it until shortly before his mind gave way). Finisher, 2026-10-03: every run of five words of the entry searched as an exact phrase in the same scan (104 searches); none was found

auden.says: He then sums the dandy up. Like a hero of poetry he depends on fortune, on money and leisure for instance; like a hero of philosophy he must have the will to make a dandy of himself from the corrupt nature every man is born with. He is no man of action and no seeker of wisdom, and wants neither the admiration of men nor the knowledge of God. His one ambition is to become conscious that he is uniquely himself and like no one else. Auden calls him the hero of religion inverted: Lucifer, who proves himself free by refusing every order, whether God’s, society’s or his own nature’s.
auden.source: Introduction to Charles Baudelaire, *Intimate Journals* (1947), pp. 19–20
auden.checked: research notes, appendix H5 and section 16; and the search snippets of the 1947 edition at archive.org, read again on 2026-10-03: the head of page 20 falls inside the sentence about the two heroes, just before the sentences on the Dandy’s ambition. Read a third time before closing, in one chain from the sentence on the opposites to the sentence that names the gratuitous act (39 steps): the Dandy makes himself out of the corrupt nature everyone is born into, and the paraphrase, which had said against it, now says from it. Finisher, 2026-10-03: the sentence on the ambition read again (three single searches of the scan through archive.org’s public full-text search, and the research notes, appendix H5). The entry could be read as giving one thing he wants to be conscious of; it now gives the two that Auden joins with “and”, in the words of the view. auden.says: Before he turns to the contrary thought, Auden names the dandy’s mistake. A man unaware of himself, he says, can rest in being by nature what no one else is. Once he is conscious of himself that is not enough, and he must set about becoming an individual in spirit. The danger then is the dandy’s mistake: to try to turn the first kind of individual into the second, and so to think that one becomes an individual in spirit by becoming unlike others, and not by becoming what one chooses to be.
auden.source: Introduction to Charles Baudelaire, *Intimate Journals* (1947), pp. 24–25

auden.says: From the start, Auden says, a line of thought runs through the journals against the dandy and his pride in being unique. He quotes two sayings: no high pleasure is unrelated to prostitution, and no being is more prostituted than God. In terms meant to provoke, Baudelaire there recognizes the Christian idea of love against the Platonic one the dandy holds. He grants that to love is to give oneself, not to desire, and that the will to become oneself can only be a will to give oneself where a neighbor needs it. Before the crisis of January 23, 1862, Auden thinks, such ideas came only now and then.
auden.source: Introduction to Charles Baudelaire, *Intimate Journals* (1947), p. 25

auden.says: His last lines are about time. By nature’s reckoning Baudelaire was too late. Seen by the spirit, he goes on, Baudelaire may be believed to have come in time: spirit needs time too, but a moment of it will do.
auden.quote: To the eye of nature, he was too late. As he spoke, the bird stooped and struck.
auden.source: Introduction to Charles Baudelaire, *Intimate Journals* (1947), p. 27; *Prose*, vol. II (2002), pp. 314–15

auden.says: He sets Baudelaire’s change of heart beside Rimbaud’s later and more showy turn from poet to trader, where he thinks the heart did not change: there, it seems to him, one kind of dandy was merely swapped for another, with the same pride and the same wish to be unique in both. Baudelaire’s humility sounds true to him because nothing showy is planned, no new career and no public farewell to poetry. Baudelaire asks in prayer only to use his gifts better.
auden.source: Introduction to Charles Baudelaire, *Intimate Journals* (1947), pp. 26–27; *Prose*, vol. II (2002), p. 314

auden.says: In *The Enchafèd Flood* the entry of January 23, 1862 is one of Auden’s instances that the hero too can perish. He quotes it in Isherwood’s translation, where *imbecility* has become *madness*. Of the dandy he says there that to the bourgeois he looks like a wild man who denies himself nothing, and that in his own eyes he is an exacting ascetic who scorns the bourgeois for being natural. He then quotes the journal on woman as the dandy’s opposite and on the dandy who should live and sleep before a looking glass.
auden.source: *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), pp. 42 and 84

auden.says: Writing on Goethe’s *Italian Journey*, he says that the aesthetic religion, as Kierkegaard named it, trusts wholly to the mood of the moment and ends in despair, and that its first stage is what Baudelaire called cultivating one’s hysteria. Writing on Tennyson, he says that Baudelaire’s error, one Tennyson did not make, was to turn the aesthetic into a religion; that his pose was a way to avoid the need for a faith and ended in disaster, in his hearing the wind that the second passage records; and that he saw it too late.
auden.source: *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973; Faber and Faber printing of 1974), pp. 136 (“Italian Journey”) and 231–32 (“Tennyson”)

caveats: Auden’s introduction of 1947 was read only in snippets of a scanned copy, not page by page. Its page numbers are counted from the page headings as that copy prints them, and several of the headings, that of page 25 among them, are garbled there.

The order of the entries is not Baudelaire’s. After his death his publisher pasted the loose sheets in an order the editors of 1908 call arbitrary, so the budget follows the dated entry only in the printed book, which is the order Auden reads.

The English printed here is Shipley’s of 1919, not the Isherwood translation that Auden set and quotes. Isherwood has *madness* where Shipley has *imbecility*, and Shipley lacks some lines of the French, among them *Trop tard peut-être*.
The French *il se dit* could be a past tense as well as a present. It is read as a present because *passent*, beside it, is present.

That no other entry gives the day of its writing is true of Shipley’s text. The French edition of 1908 has a list of errands headed with a day of 1856 and a quoted sentence with its date in 1863; Shipley has neither.
open: The order of the leaves is not Baudelaire’s. The editors of 1908, following Eugène Crépet, say the journals were made up after his death by his publisher Poulet-Malassis from loose, unnumbered sheets, pasted in an order they call necessarily arbitrary. That the budget of the third plate was written after the warning of the second is the order of the printed book, and Auden’s reading; the one day of writing given in Shipley’s text is January 23, 1862.

Auden’s introduction of 1947 was read in the research notes and in search-inside snippets of a lending-only scan at archive.org, not page by page. Its page numbers come from the running heads as the scan’s text prints them: 19, 20 and 26 are clear and 27 is damaged. Shipley’s text differs from the French in places the plates touch. He prints Jean for Jeanne. His a few hours on the third plate stands for plusieurs heures, several hours. After the question that breaks off, the French of 1908 has a line his text lacks, about glory, the paying of his debts, and wealth for Jeanne and his mother. The leaf before the budget opens in French with a line his text lacks: too late perhaps; his mother and Jeanne; his own health as a matter of charity and duty; Jeanne’s illnesses; his mother’s infirmities and solitude. The capital in Stole on the first plate is in the Project Gutenberg text (line 7545 of .cache/texts/pg47032_baudelaire.txt) and not in the book. Finisher, 2026-10-03: two scans of the 1919 book at archive.org, read in their full text (baudelairehispro00baud, a Modern Library printing, and baudelairehispro00baudiala), print the word with a small letter, and so do the search snippets of three more scans (baudelairehispro0000tbsm, baudelairehispro0000unse, and baudelairehispro00baud_0, dated 1925). Lead, 2026-10-03: the text printed here is mended from the book where it is built (build/texts/baudelaire.mjs, SLIPS), and the note on the book in the reader says so; the caveat’s sentence on the capital and the clause in what the French tab stands on are out again.

That no other entry gives the day of its writing is true of Shipley’s text. The French of 1908 has one more dated leaf, a list of errands headed Tuesday, May 13, 1856, and a quotation dated November 7, 1863; Shipley’s text has neither.

The French shown on the first plate is the Project Gutenberg e-text, which prints two hyphens for a dash, has lost the first dash of the aside and has no quotation marks around the man’s question. The Paris edition of 1908 prints both dashes and the quotation marks. The two French editions and Shipley number the entries differently: his XXVI is XV in the e-text.

The form il se dit could be a past tense as well as a present. It is read here as a present because passent, beside it, is present, and because Isherwood’s translation also keeps the present and the reflexive.

The sonnet Le Gouffre was read in the edition of 1868. An earlier printing in the review L’Artiste on March 1, 1862, five weeks after the dated entry, is given by one web page that cites the Pléiade edition; it was not checked further, and the caption gives no date for the sonnet.

The stroke of 1866 rests on Wikipedia alone. The Oxford English Dictionary was not consulted; English dates are from the Online Etymology Dictionary. French senses are from Littré, whose dictionary littre.org dates to the late nineteenth century, later than these notes. The page numbers of The Enchafèd Flood and of Forewords and Afterwords are those of the printings scanned (Vintage Books, 1967; Faber and Faber, 1974).
